To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the equated score distributions are similar across the various equating/scaling method combinations, but systematic differences exist that would lead to classification differences for individual examinees.

the two equating techniques (TSE and ETE) produced different equated scores for the same examinees, and that the differences in scores were systematic and could have important implications in the interpretation of the scores.

(a) ETE tended to produce higher scores than TSE; (b) the scaling method within equating method combinations had a greater effect on equated scores than the equating method within scaling method combinations; (c) the equating method had a greater effect across scaling methods than the scaling method had across equating methods; and (d) the scaling method had a greater influence on the classification of examineees into performance categories than the equating methods.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the consistency of equated scores and the comparability of the equating methods.

the comparability of the equated scores resulting from two equating methods and six scaling methods, as well the comparability of examinees' placement into performance categories based on the equated scores.
the comparability of equating methods and scaling methods.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the equating methods/scaling methods combinations examined in this study do not yield identical results.
TSE and ETE produce different classifications of examinees into ability groups.

ETE and TSE are not equivalent equating methods, but the degree of difference in equating scores is not trivial and would likely have an impact on the classification of examinee performance categories.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the differences in the equating methods were not large, but they were not trivial either, and that the differences in scaling methods within equating methods were more pronounced
the choice of equating/scaling method has the potential to influence the classification of examinee into performance categories.

the use of IRT based equating methods and the selection of scaling method within equating method should not be taken lightly, as they can have an impact on the interpretation of the results of a test administration.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of multiple equating methods and scaling methods is warranted when equating test forms, and that the use of a single equating/scaling method is likely to result in systematic differences in the scores obtained for examinees.
the choice of equating method and scaling method may influence the interpretation of examinee performance.
the use of different equating methods and scaling methods may lead to different classifications of examinees into categories, which may lead to differential decisions.
